messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh, a 35-year-old South Eastern Asian American UX designer, had always thought of himself as disciplined and dependable, the sort of person who could manage deadlines, clients, and long stretches at a screen without making a fuss. That sense of himself changed after a life-threatening illness that began abruptly enough that, in the months that followed, he often replayed the first moments as if they belonged to someone else. What he remembers most clearly is the hospital smell, the rushing movement of ambulances and staff, and the overwhelming feeling that his body had become unreliable without warning. He was admitted through an emergency department after he became seriously ill, and the experience of being examined, monitored, and waiting for updates while strangers discussed his condition left a lasting mark. Even after he recovered physically, the memory stayed vivid in a way that felt intrusive and unwelcome to him. He found himself returning to it in fragments, then stopping himself because thinking about it at all made him feel as if he were back in the hospital again.

In the weeks after discharge, Minh began to organize his life around not having to encounter anything that reminded him of that period. He avoided hospitals completely, even when passing one on the way to work, and would cross the street or look down so he did not have to register the entrance or the sight of an ambulance outside. He also resisted medical appointments and physical examinations as much as he could, delaying routine care and telling himself that if he did not put his body in that setting, he would not have to face the same fear again. At home, he shut down conversations that drifted toward illness, hospitalization, or what had happened to him, because thinking about the event made his chest tighten and brought back the sense that something catastrophic was about to happen. He noticed that he was equally reluctant to do anything that made his body feel taxed. If an activity raised his heart rate or left him short of breath, he backed away quickly, choosing the safer option of rest over pushing himself, because he had come to associate bodily stress with danger.

As the months passed, Minh became increasingly alert to signs that something might be wrong. At work, where he spent long hours as a UX designer moving between design reviews, screen work, and meetings, he found himself unsettled by delays that others barely noticed. If a teammate took longer than expected to reply, if a server response lagged, or if a meeting started late, his mind immediately jumped to the possibility that something bad was happening. He would wait tensely, scanning for updates, unable to settle until he knew more. Even when his wife tried to reassure him that everything was fine, he found it almost impossible to believe her. Reassurance did not seem to reach the part of him that stayed on guard. His body often felt braced for impact, muscles tight and ready to react, as if he were still waiting for the next medical emergency to announce itself.

Minh had also begun to think about himself in harsher terms than he used to. The illness had left him feeling exposed and ashamed, and he increasingly interpreted his reactions as proof that there was something wrong with him as a person. He described feeling weak, not only because his body had failed him, but because he could not simply “move on” the way he believed other people might. That sense of weakness sat alongside a kind of emotional deadness that disturbed him almost as much. There were moments when he realized he was going through work, meals, and conversations without really feeling present in them, as though some part of him had gone numb after the illness and never fully returned. He worried that his wife could see this change, and although he remained engaged in daily life, he also felt increasingly separate from it, as if he were functioning from a distance.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become difficult to ignore. He was still working, but the effort of avoiding reminders, monitoring his body, and staying composed was wearing him down. The turning point came after a recent situation in which a medical-related prompt and a delayed update at work left him tense for hours, unable to settle and increasingly convinced that trouble was coming. He recognized that his world had grown smaller around the fear of hospitals, examinations, and anything that might strain his body, and that his marriage was beginning to absorb the strain of his constant vigilance and withdrawal. Minh came to therapy hoping to understand why the illness still felt so present and why he felt both numb and on edge at the same time. More than anything, he wanted to believe that he could be safe in his own body again, though what frightened him most was the thought that the threat would never fully leave him.
